vignette:
Arthur, a 72-year-old North American man who had spent most of his career as a software engineer, came to treatment describing how a captivity years earlier still organized his days. He had been taken and tortured in circumstances he did not describe in full at first, only saying that during that time he was forced to endure acts that made him feel he had been stripped of every safeguard and pushed into behavior that went against who he was. In the months after he escaped, what stayed with him most was not only the pain and fear of the event itself but the conviction that something in him had been permanently altered. He spoke in a flat, controlled way about having lost faith in people and in any larger order that might keep cruelty from happening again, and he often said he felt set apart from everyone else, as though other people lived in a world that still made sense while he did not.

That sense of rupture fed directly into the way Arthur tried to manage his mind. He had come to believe that if he did not keep close watch over every thought, he might lose control or "go crazy," so he monitored himself constantly, measuring each intrusive image against what he considered normal and alarming himself when his mind drifted toward the torture. Because he felt he had acted in ways that violated his values, he made an effort to suppress any thought that might remind him of what had happened, fearing that even remembering it meant he was somehow tainted by it. His isolation sharpened that effort: living alone in his apartment, he would sit in silence and work hard not to think, as though any unguarded moment might let the past flood back and prove that he was no longer the person he had been.

At the same time, Arthur had become relentlessly alert to danger in the present. He studied people's faces and body language with a software engineer's habit of pattern detection, scanning for the slightest hardening of the jaw, the narrowing of the eyes, or a shift in posture that might signal menace. In his building he repeatedly checked the front door, the windows, and the locks before he could settle, and on some nights he would make another circuit of the apartment before bed because he needed to feel certain nothing could get in. Sleep had become difficult because he felt he had to stay alert; even when he was exhausted, he lay in bed listening for footsteps in the hall or the click of the latch, convinced that lowering his guard was dangerous.

The more he watched for threat, the more certain he became that his earlier experience had revealed something permanent about the world. When he noticed a stranger staring too long in a grocery line or a neighbor's face seeming unreadable, he took it as confirmation that people could not be trusted. Those moments fed his belief that he had been fundamentally violated and left him isolated from others, because if cruelty could be hidden behind ordinary faces, then no one was safe and no relationship could be fully relied upon. In response, he tightened the habits that had already formed: he kept scrutinizing his own thoughts for signs of collapse, pushed away memories as soon as they surfaced, and avoided being alone in a room or building unless he could first reassure himself that every exit and lock had been checked.

Over time, these routines had carved down his life. At work, where he still did some consulting from home, he found himself distracted by the need to look at the screen, then at his own thoughts, then back to the door, and he had begun turning down opportunities that would require him to be in unfamiliar offices or to stay late in an empty building. He was embarrassed by how often he avoided being alone and how much time he spent checking locks, but he also believed that letting these habits lapse would expose him to danger or to a breakdown he might not recover from. That belief kept him trapped in the same cycle: the more he tried to suppress the memory and monitor his mind, the more alien he felt, and the more alien he felt, the more he concluded that he had indeed been changed by the torture in a way that set him apart from everyone else.

By the time he sought help, Arthur was exhausted by the strain of keeping himself under such constant surveillance. What finally brought him in was a stretch of nights when he could not fall asleep at all without repeatedly getting up to check the doors and windows, followed by a morning when he found himself staring at a colleague's face on a video call and realizing he was no longer hearing the words because he was studying every expression for threat. He came in hoping to learn how to quiet the vigilance and the thought-monitoring, but he was most afraid that if he stopped scanning himself and others, he would either be harmed again or discover that the torture had indeed broken something permanent in him.
